Mr. PAUL MERCIER (St. Henri) presented the first report of the special committee appointed to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise as follows:
Your committee recommend that leave be granted them to employ counsel for the purpose of assisting in the investigation of the matters referred to them.
He said:	With the consent of the House,
I beg to move:
That the first report of the special committee appointed to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise be concurred in.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
criminal, naturallly falls into two phases. There are on the one side those seeking to bring home guilt, wrongdoing, irregularity or whatever it may be, while there are on the other side those who endeavour t<5 remove inferences of guilt, that is to say, dn a word, to defend the case. That is the way all trials are conducted. Experience has shown that these divisions inevitaJbly occur; and if counsel are to be employed for the committee, if the committee feels that it cannot undertake the labour-and I can quite understand that there would 'be very much labour entailed in the study of documents, the systematizing of evidence and exhibits, and all that-then surely it would have been in the interests of justice and of tlhe arrival at the truth if the committee had followed the regular course and had one counsel prosecuting the investigation, analogous to prosecution anywhere, and another counsel representing the other side.
I do not think anything in the world can be gained by appointing a common counsel for the committee. It seems to me that the experience of last session, when what was alleged to be counsel for the committee was appointed in the Petersen investigation, should have been a warning to the House not to follow that process on a subsequent occasion. I should very much have preferred had the committee come before us with a request for counsel, the intention being that the regular course should be followed and that counsel on either side be appointed. I do not think that members of the committee are entitled to counsel at all, whether it be those representing us in this end of the chamber, those representing the government, or those representing the Progressive party; members of the committee are no more entitled to counsel than is a judge entitled to legal advice as to what he ought to do. It is the public that is entitled to counsel; the public is interested not only in the bringing out of the facts but in seeing as well that no injustice is done in the elucidation of those facts. The government is justified in employing counsel in the public interests and not, in the interests of the committee nor as specially representative of any members of the committee. I am sorry that this view has not prevailed in the committee, and I apprehend that if what has been stated to me as the decision of the committee in the matter of counsel be followed, and if this motion passes, 
the investigation will turn out to be unsatisfactory. Certainly the relation of counsel to the investigation will be unsatisfactory and the public interest will not be served.
Is it not true that the members of the committee have concurred in the terms agreed upon?
I understand that they have agreed, but the agreement has come only after the other plan along the lines I have urged was overborne.

I hardly understand some of the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). The right hon. gentleman speaks about prosecution and defence, but I understood that this was to be a committee of investigation to get at the facts of the case and that there was no suggestion of either prosecution or defence. I think the leader of the opposition has the wrong view.

I listened with a good deal of interest and, at first, with sympathy to what the leader of the opposition said. What struck me as of great force was that the people should be represented, and- it has just occurred to me that the members of the committee really represent the people and for that reason are entitled to counsel. Is not that a fair way of looking at the question?

I thought I had made myself clear. Certainly as members of parliament they represent the people; but a judge, too, represents the people in the exercise of his jurisdiction. Every investigation before a court, whether it be a civil or a criminal case, is an inquiry into facts, just as this investigation is; and every inquiry as to facts is best conducted when one end takes the prosecution and the other the defence. Experience has shown that this is the best course to pursue. Every inquiry, as I have pointed out, falls into these two divisions and it cannot be otherwise; that has been the history of jurisprudence in all countries. Now why should this be different from any other investigation? I am not urging counsel at all, although I know they are good counsel. But if the committee feels that there should be counsel then there is no reason for departing in this investigation from what time has proven to be the right method in all investigations as to facts, whether the facts appertain to a criminal or to a civil dispute.

How many counsel are to be employed and for whom are they to act?
One.
Is there to be any counsel representing the other side?

Does not the position taken by the leader of the opposition imply that the committee must of necessity divide itself into two parts, one portion of the committee being inclined to assume the role of prosecutors and the other that of defenders? I take it that the committee and the House ought not so to divide. I understand that at least one member of the committee does not occupy any such position and if that gentleman is to be a sort of judge in the matter, then I would say that whether we have counsel representing either prosecution or defence, we should decidedly have counsel to represent as far as possible the interests of the people irrespective of party.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Does a judge in a civil or in a criminal trial divide himself into two parts? Well, the committee is the judge.

Decidedly he does
not. That is the very reason why the committee should not so divide itself.
But there are counsel on each side in any proceeding before a judge, civil or criminal.
I do not want to trespass, Mr. Speaker, but I would suggest the trouble is we are turning a parliamentary committee into a court.
That is what it is.
That is almost inevitable.

Mr. Speaker, I regret I was not in my seat when this discussion began. Since the committee has been sitting I have reached the conclusion that we ought to have counsel representing the Conservative party, the Liberal party and myself respectively.
Now it is coming out. We ought to have three counsel.

We met
yesterday in camera, but I was overridden. The recommendation now made I moved in
the committee this morning in deference to the unanimous opinion of the other members. Of cotirse. if the House is opposed to the recommendation, well and good; but this recommendation expresses the opinion of the committee that, so far as the committee itself is concerned, we ought to have counsel possibly more than one.
In the light of what the bon, minister has said, may I ask why it is that the services of Mr. Geoffrion are being continued? The minister says the department has no defence to make.

The services of Mr. Geoffrion are being continued in the interests of the Department of Customs because so far no other counsel has been appointed, and not until we are thoroughly convinced that it is the intention of the new counsel to probe the administration of the department very thoroughly, noit only during the past year but during the past eight, ten, twelve or perhaps twenty yeans, will we dispense with the services of the counsel already retained.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) has just said that the committee this morning unanimously decided that counsel should be retained to assist them. This places me in a better position than I would be in if members of the committee who sit on this side of the House had themselves recommended this course. Now, I may be wrong, but I do not see the necessity for counsel. The hon. member for \ ancouver Centre has brought charges against the Department of Customs and Excise, and it is up to him to prove those charges; it is not the duty of the committee to find witnesses for him. The committee is acting as judge of the evidence to be adduced before it. If the hon. member few- Vancouver Centre has no evidence to bring forward, so much the worse for him; but the committee has nothing to do with that. The Minister of Customs drafted the order of reference in such wide and ample terms as to give the hon. member every facility to substantiate his charges. The duty of the committee is to hear the evidence and report upon it to the House, and having done so its powers are exhausted. In the last resort, it is for this House to determine whether or not that report shall be accepted or rejected, or to send it back to the committee with certain instructions. That is the procedure. I repeat, Sir, that I cannot see the necessity of retaining counsel to act on behalf of the committee.
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (South Wellington) ; Mr. Speaker, it is quite true, as the hon. Minister of Customs has stated, that the motion to appoint the Customs committee was made by the government. But it is equally true, and within the knowledge of everyone in the House, that certain charges were made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre of maladministration in the Department of Customs-
I said that.

-and it was in respect
of those charges, some of them very definite and very positive, that this committee of investigation was appointed. Personally I would have no objection Whatever to the employment of counsel by the Department of Customs; I think under all the circumstances that is their right. But there is another side to the case-the public. Now, the public are concerned. My hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. Denis) stated that the member for Vanoouver Centre had made certain definite charges. He certainly has made some very broad charges. My hon. friend from Joliette lays the burden on the shoulders of the hon. member of proving those charges. Surely, then, he should have something to say in regard to the prosecution of those charges before the committee. I think we are all well aware that three members of the committee represent the government side of the House-*
Four.

-four members of the committee represent the opposition side, and one member represents the Progressive side. My information is only gained in the corridors, but I understand it was insisted that every one of those political parties should have counsel-for what purpose I hardly know. The idea to me was absurd, and I so expressed myself when I heard it. One party of members representing the government to have counsel, another party of members representing the opposition to have counsel, and the third and single member representing the Progressive party to have counsel! Surely that is not in the interests of justice, of fair play or of anything else. My hon. friend from Joliette, said he would be prepared to accept the proposition that no counsel be employed'. Were it not for the tremendous amount of work that is to be performed, I think his suggestion would be a good one, and that the committee might deal with the matter themselves without counsel. But in this case there is so much involved and there are so many ramifications to be dealt with that I doubt if any nine men could do justice to the case without the reasonable assistance of counsel. If there is to be counsel for the committee one should suffice, but I think my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre should be the one to name that counsel. The government, or the Minister of Customs at the present time, has employed counsel, which I think is proper.
Hear, hear.

Surely then he will allow
those who have laid the charges, who have

120,000	tons to be mined and banked for future delivery to 135,000 tons, the additional 15,000 tons to be mined at the Princess mine. Just the other day he informed me that they had received word that the mining company were not prepared to increase that order by 15,000 tons; in other words they were not prepared to bank that coal. That was the state-
The Address-Mr. Cahan

meat I received from Mr. Vaughan. I do not recollect, but I think I am safe in saying that the excuse given was that it was going to cost too much money. On the Orders of the Day:

I call the attention of the government to a report that fifty families of immigrants are being settled on lands on the Fraser river, British Columbia, lately vacated by soldier settlers who were not able to make their payments. I understand these immigrants are being settled there at valuations less than those originally placed upon the lands. I should like to inquire whether it is a fact that immigrants are being settled on vacated soldier settlers' lands, at valuations below those originally placed on the lands, and if that is the. fact, why those lands are not revalued1 for our own soldiers who formerly occupied them or who now occupy them?

With
reference to the first question, I will have to get the information from the Soldier Settlement Board. More than that, I repeat that the leader of the House cannot at the present time state that he has .one single public measure ready to submit to this House. If he has such a measure, and if he is willing that this House shall proceed with the despatch of business. Mr. Speaker, if hon.
gentlemen opposite have any sense of fairness-*

If t'he hon. member for
St. Lawrence-St. George does not wish to be interrupted that is his privilege. The rule is well known. An hon. member addressing the House and -not wishing to be interrupted is within his right in declining to yield the floor.

I 'have no objection to
feeing interrupted in the ordinary course of events, but when the hon. gentleman propounds questions for the mere purpose of creating a turmoil and disorder almost unprecedented in this assembly I ignore his interruptions.
On the issue between myself, and those who are of the same opinion as I, and hon. gentlemen opposite, we on this side are unanimously agreed that this government is utterly incapable of carrying on 4 p.m. the public business of the country.
It has demonstrated that clearly by refusing day by day, and week by week, to introduce one public measure -for our consideration. Furthermore if there were any doubt in the mind of any hon. member here, if there were any doubt in the mind of any person in this country as to the utility-and not only the utility but the absolute necessity-of this parliament functioning while the special committee investigating into the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise is conducting its inquiry, I think it ~was disclosed here to-day how absolutely necessary it is. It is absolutely necessary in order that there may be a full investigation into those matter's which resulted-according to the estimate I think, of the right hon. Prime Minister a year ago-in some $50,000,000 of defalcations in the public revenues of Canada. Therefore I say that hon. gentlemen *opposite will not meet wiitlh very substantial support from the public of Canada when they talk about the expense into which we are plunging the country in continuing this debate, and in continuing to consider the -matters which were presented to us by His Excellency the Governor General in his Speech from the Throne.
When parliament w-as convened there was a phrase in the message received from His Excellency the Governor General which was in accordance with (the tradition and practice of -parliament for all time. It was that phrase in which he announced, through his deputy, that he did not see fit to declare the causes of his summoning the present parliament of Canada (until (the Speaker of the House of Commons should -have been chosen according to law. He then indicated to this parliament that upon our choice of a Speaker to

The Address-Mr. Cahan
preside at our assembly, he would, in accordance with ancient practice and tradition, declare the causes of his summoning the present parliament of Canada. Unfortunately His Excellency the Governor General may speak only such words as are committed to him, by the Prime Minister of Canada for expression, and when we met we had the declaration by hon, gentlemen opposite that parliament was convened, for what? Did they declare that parliament had been convened in order that the assembled members might decide whether the government, in the shattered condition in which it was, Still had the confidence of this parliament? The one thing which is absolutely necessary in our governmental institutions is that the Prime Minister shall deal with absolute frankness with His Excellency the Governor General and this parliament in all matters that are placed on the lips of His Excellency. Therefore, that statement, if properly presented, we agreed, might have been a matter upon whidh this House might decide, upon which., if there were any doubt about- the matter in the minds of hon. gentlemen, they might call upon the members of this House to decide. But no such intimation appears in the Speech of His Excellency to parliament. It was not even intimated that parliament was asked to decide upon that question, and if there -were any doubt about the matter, the Prime Minister had no authority whatever to present to this House a .Speech from the Throne until that preliminary question had been decided by the House. That was very clearly stated by the hon. member for West York OSir Henry Drayton) when he referred to May's Parliamentary Practice, twelfth edition, at page 143, and showed that the proper practice, in case the House was convened to enable parliament to decide whether or not the government woluld be sustained, was to 'postpone the' delivery of His Excellency's Speech and to invite the House to decide that question upon the government's record and not upon the entirely new promises set forth in the Speech from the Throne. Hon. gentlemen opposite abandoned the precepts of the constitution and they introduced a new message which is now before us.
I took some pains yesterday to read to the House at great length the official declaration made by the Prime Minister of -the considerations which he had presented to His Excellency when asking for a dissolution of parliament. I also gave from the mouth of the Prime Minister a complete and detailed statement of the issues upon which he appealed to this country. He also stated, in those addresses at Richmond1 Hill and Erindale, that 14011-71
he was prepared to appeal to and to abide by the decision of the people on the issues which he then -presented. But when c(ur hon. friends who now form the remnant of the government became parties to the presentation to this House of an address, under the circumstances under which they presented it, they omitted every single consideration which had been presented by the Prime Minister bo His Excellency as a reason for dissolution. They omitted every ground upon which they had appealed to the people before, and by abrogating, annulling and refusing to follow the proper parliamentary practice, they came in with their bids for political support on grounds that they had never before dared to place before parliament and the people of this country. I told hon. gentlemen the other night some of the' evils which were bound to flow from Such an utter disregard of the precepts and practice of the constitution, and the result is this: They -have themselves introduced anarchy into this House and they cannot complain if, within the rules, members on this side show that it is impossible for this mutilated' government to function.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen opposite may laugh, but this country is not laughing. This country from one end to the other is in a state of the greatest anxiety, in a state of business depression, in a state in which the people are looking forward to ascertain if some stable government can be given them. Old enterprises are being curtailed, new enterprises are not being undertaken. From day to day it has been suggested by hon. members, whether they be from British Columbia, Hamilton, or Sydney, that under industrial conditions which prevail, men, women and children are in destitution and starving to death in this country, and that starvation and destitution will continue so long as this defunct government undertakes, against the will of the people, the functions of government which they are utterly incapable of exercising and which, if they attempt to exercise, they must exercise in so inefficient a manner as to disgust men, women and children throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

I am not answering questions this afternoon as I want to finish my remarks before midnight. Hon. gentlemen yesterday persisted in asking me questions; they took up the whole of the time of the

House, and then they blamed and condemned me for wasting the public moneys of the country. There never was, and, I trust there never will be again in the history of Canada, a debate under conditions such as those which now prevail-a long adjournment ahead; but it means that we are debating practically without additional cost to this country. have a cut aggregating $300 a day made in their wages. If that be so, instead of working here without additional or further cost we are working at one-third the usual cost, because services of the kind I indicate run to about $900 a day while the House is in session.

Then he works himself up to a superlative degree of enthusiasm when he pictures the Right Hon. Mr. King as vanquishing the Meighen ideas out in Prince Albert. It is a first-rate, wonderful achievement to lick an opponent when you have the field all to yourself. This splendid victory that is so lauded-this return of the vanquished Prime Minister, who had been defeated where he was known, where he had been sitting, yes, where he was within striking distance-was achieved by his having the field all to himself-no Conservative candidate to oppose him.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen laugh, but I would ask them whether the Progressive was a Liberal candidate in Grenville in 1922. These vacant laughs ought to stop unless hon. gentlemen are prepared to make that admission. They know that there was no Conservative candidate in that by-election in Prince Albert. The right hon. gentleman had the field to himself and the hon. member now rises to heights of enthusiasm over what he considers the defeat of Meighen principles. Mr. Speaker, it really is to laugh. I have no intention of entering into a general political debate, although the door has been left wide open to me through the kindly offices of the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird). But before going into the details of the incident I am going to make one or two general submissions which perhaps may not be quite out of place even as applied to this government. Has the country the right to expect from the government frankness in the statements which it makes? Has the country the right to rely upon the word of the government? Or is that word a light and fragile thing, the scattered pieces of which, when it is broken, can be put together again by some of that mysterious cement which is to be provided at the expense of the ratepayers of Canada, the cement that binds together various groups in this House? Again, has the country still the right to expect that affairs shall be so conducted that it will be enabled to put credence in the government? And if it is impossible for the people to place any credence in the government, is not ' that fact sufficient fully to justify even party supporters of the government in voting a lack of confidence in it? Is the government supposed to hold public credit and public cash inviolate except upon the order of this House, or is that, too, something that is to be lightly regarded?
I propose discussing for a few minutes the methods which this government have adopted in the building of railways when they want to build them-railways which they do not want the Senate to defeat, railways which they want to build without this House knowing anything about them. These things of course are done very much under cover. During the last campaign one of the strongest points taken in western territory by the present member elect for Prince Albert was his attack upon the Senate, and one of the chief reasons for that attack, a reason that appealed particularly to western ears, was the assertion that railways which were essential to the proper development of the west had been thrown out by the upper house. The right hon. gentleman did not take the farmers of the west into his confidence and tell them how, when he was considering the requirements of other and more favoured individuals, he could ingeniously arrange matters when it paid him to do so. He did not tell them that. I refer to governmental methods in connection with the building of the Rouyn railway. Now I want to make it absolutely clear that what I am objecting to in this connection is the method which was adopted. The district itself, I believe, is a splendid one.
I do not think that the mineral wealth of the
[Sir Henry Drayton.)
country is confined to northern Ontario; the belt will be found to run right through into Quebec. I have no doubt about it, and development in that country will and ought to achieve a success equal to the success that has been attained in other parts of Ontario. I am not arguing that simply because this country's credit has been strained, simply because many people to-day are of the opinion that our railway deficits are heavier than we have a right to expect them to be, we should therefore put a stop to further extensions. Nor am I suggesting that we should have done nothing in the matter inasmuch as the province of Ontario was willing to save us the cost. Not at all. This issue is not one that can be veiled by provincial interest or prejudice or anything else, and it has nothing to do with the question whether or not the particular country is one through which a railway ought to be built. Unless you want to increase further the deficits on the National Railways, why must traffic be carried forty-five miles up north, to be 'taken again forty-five miles south, with the inverse extra mileage on the return movement? I do not want to go into that. I want to make it perfectly clear that none of these questions need be given the slightest attention, having regard to the matters I purpose urging. What I do intend to go into is the method by which this government deceives and flouts parliament and the people -the method by which it did do so in this particular question. Then I am going to ask the House whether they like that sort of thing, whether the cement is sufficiently strong to reunite over the chasm wrought by such practice as hon. gentlemen opposite engage in in relation to those whose co-operation they have received up to the present.

Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham):

have suggested to capitalists that if they would build a branch line between two points to be named by the Canadian National, one of them being Rouyn, the company would be prepared to lease that line.

It would occur to me that with the elections over the secrecy of the past, even on the lowest political grounds, need be no longer observed and the mystery surrounding this matter which is, after all, a public undertaking and one wherein the members of the cabinet are risking not their own but public monies, ought to be dissipated.
I was in hopes that you would be able to give me a definite answer to my telephonic request before now. May I have either the orders in council or information as to when they will be obtainable.

The government did not get from this House the authority to guarantee the bonds of the Rouyn Rail-

lease ia hereinafter called "the said lease", and to cause it to be operated as a part of the Canadian National
Railways;
And whereas it is anticipated that during the first few years after the said line of railway has been completed and opened for traffic deficits will arise in connection with the operation thereof;
And whereas the province of Quebec is willing to guarantee the payment against such deficits, if any, of $50,000 a year for five years from the date the said line of railway is opened for traffic, hereinafter called the "initial date,'" but a further guarantee is required of $20,000 a year for the same period from the guarantor who is interested in mining locations to be reached by the said line of railway.
After the delays to which I was subjected and of which I fully informed' the House this afternoon, if I have now got everything that has to do with this precious excursion of the government into this field of operations, the facts would seem to show that they were in an indecent haste to push this railway on for purposes known only to themselves but very strongly suspected to have some political significance in relation to the last election. This very document shows that the Quebec government is to guarantee deficits to the extent of 850,000 per annum, and the government's haste was such that the order in council was passed and the work rushed on apparently without a single thing being done by the government of that province. I do not know whether that is true or not, but what I am stating is that I have here all the papers I could get and there is not one line here to indicate that the necessary legislative authority had been obtained by the Quebec government or that this government had received their bond. I call the attention of the House to Striking evidence which we have before us of the fact that it is the government that is doing all this in the guise of a phantom company. I invite your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the first covenant:
His Majesty agrees-
Olh, what crimes are committed in the name of the King! What a pity it is that our constitutional forms require His Majesty's name to be attached to documents of this kind. However, His Majesty the King is made to agree:
(1)	To cause the railway company to construct and complete the said line of railway with all reasonable expedition and to lease it from the railway company by le^se approximately in the form attached.
Could clearer proof be obtained of what I now charge? This construction is the work of this government: is it possible to get anything clearer in proof of that fact than we have here? Is it possible to make it more clear that this work is the work of this government, executed under subterfuge and carried on under sluch a condition as to amount

absolutely to a misleading, a misguiding and a flouting of the privileges and the jurisdiction of parliament? Could the evidence be more conclusive? The government agrees to cause the railway company to construct and complete the line of railway " with all reasonable expedition There is an old legal maxim which probably hon. gentlemen have forgotten:
Qui facit per alium facit per se.
And many a criminal has done time under that same doctrine-Who does it through another does it himself. Everyone knows that, and here is this government building this railway through a phantom company. The next clause reads:
(2) To cause the operation of the said line of railway when leased to be entrusted to the Canadian National Railway Company for operation under the terms of section 11 of chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada 1919.
(3)	To cause accounts to be kept of all freight traffic moving over the said line of railway and/or freight traffic originating upon or destined to points upon the said line of railway moving from, through or to points upon the Canadian National Railways in Canada, all such traffic being hereinafter called "such traffic."
(4)	To allocate 30 per cent of the gross earnings received by the Canadian National Railways from such traffic, hereinafter called "the said operating net earnings," to the said line of railway as earnings attributable to said line of railway for the purposes of this agreement.
I said that the shareholders need not be unduly alarmed. I wonder if the House appreciates for one moment what is being done here. Here we have a line of railway 45 miles long to connect with the main line. It is very much the short haul, and its rates and expenses will be of course in proportion to that short haul. Now railway ratios are stubborn things, although very simple, and sometimes we fail to realize their full import. We have to remember that the operating ratio of a railway applies to the dollar: it costs so much to earn the dollar. Supposing we take the earnings at a dollar and expenses at 90 cents, there of course we have an operating ratio of 90; that means we have a profit of 10 cents out of each dollar. Supposing we take from that dollar 30 cents- as is proposed under this so-called guarantee -the dollar would become 70 cents, the expenses would be just the same, 90 cents; but the operating ratio, instead of showing a profit of 10 cents for each dollar's worth of business, would become 128.75, making a loss for each dollar's worth of business done of 28.75 cents. I think everybody knows that the Transcontinental is not a paying proposition for this country. But the effect of this agreement is that before the company can

The Address-Sir Henry Drayton
be called.1 upon to pay five cents towards the deficit, that 30 cents is to be taken away, not from the net-that would not apply, of course, in the case I have been giving- but from the gross earnings, insufficient as they are now to support the property. I wonder why they did not make it fifty per cent at once. Well, I think with the thirty they are probably just as safe as if they had made it fifty, because it seems to me there would have to be an awful lot of bad management, improper expenses of construction and the like, before even this line could be in such a bad position that after getting thirty per cent of all the long-haul National business there would be a shortage on its own short-haul business.
Let us look into it a little closer, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian National Railway's figures are not complete for the year, but I think 1925 can be fairly said to be the best operating year they have had'. Nevertheless the operating ratio of all National lines down to the end of November last amounted to 87.831. Of course, 'the little business off this line would only go to a small extent in that large pool, but to the extent it did go let us take the local business and assume it was good enough-which it !3 not; I am making a violent assumption in favour of the local business-to show an operating ratio of 87.83, and just see what happens. If we take that dollar gross revenue, which we now have on actual figures, with expenses of 87.83, and if we take the thirty per cent off that dollar, thus pulling it down to 70 cents, we then have an operating ratio of 125.52. In other words, we lose 25.52 cents for every dollar's worth of business we do. instead of making 12.17 cents.
Let us look at it now from the other way and see while the government system is penalized on the one hand, and how the receipts of this local system are to be built up on the other. Supposing we have receipts for the local line and expenses worked out in ratio of 840 to 860. we would have a ratio of 150- spending $1.50 to earn $1. Supposing on the other hand you take the exact situation here and add 30 per cent of the long haul gross, your expenses remain at the sixty, and you at once have a profitable undertaking. But all that has to be done before five cents is to be taken from the Noranda company. As I said before. I do not think the Noranda shareholders need be at all anxious-yes, I am inclined to think, as has been suggested to me, Mr. Speaker, that they are just as safe as the stenographers of the Canadian National Railway Company who incorporated the railway. I notice this is to go on and there 14011-72
are to be periods for accounting and the like -I will not bother the House with the details.
That gets us down to the .point where we have the suggestion coming from somebody in this government to the stenographers of the Rouyn Railway Company that the govem-men is willing to do business with them. Acting on that suggestion, we have the lease and we have the agreement with the mining company. The next exhibit produced is an extract from the minutes of a meeting of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways held in the company's office in the city of Montreal, on June 9, 1925, reading as follows:
With regard to the proposed Rouyn branch, Mr. Rayside reported to the meeting that the matter had been gone into further with representatives of the Quebec government, who had promised that free right of way over Quebec crown lands would be given, together with any timber on such lands, and that other interested parties may increase their contribution to $20,000 per year for five years.
It was unanimously resolved that if the said line be constructed by another company, with free right of way on Quebec government lands as above referred to, and if there be contributed annually for five years $50,000 by the Quebec government and $20,000 by other interested parties, such payments aggregating $350,000 in all, and if the said line were leased for a long term of years to the Dominion government and by it entrusted to the Canadian National Railways for operation, and if said payments are made direct to the Canadian National Railways as representing the said lessee, and if the rental under the lease would represent not more than 6 per cent on the cost of construction, the directors would approve of such construction and leasing and entrusting.
That ties up the Canadian National management to the operation of the line. Their consent is there given. The amusing thing about it is that while again this thing is drawn as a matter of form for the purpose of deceiving the people, carrying the pretence right through,, truth will out every now and again, and truth emerges here, for the minutes start with the statement:
With regard to the proposed Rouyn branch.
Whose branch? What branch? If it had been a line for that company it would have been described as that company's line. If it is a branch of the Canadian National Railways,

well, truth will out, and it is stated to be their branch. If anything further was wanted to show the deception, here it is. The shadow is lifting, the pretence is disappearing. We have an application in Quebec to-day to change the name of the company to the Canadian National Branch Lines Company. It may take a little while to get the truth, but it is coming. We have another thing in these exhibits. Some people like to have the cash to play with-yes, and sometimes do something more than play with

it. Here is a work that was to be done by contract in the autumn of the year. Anybody who knows anything about railway contracting knows that a very substantial sum of money has to be put into the work before any payments are made at all. If you are really in the contracting business, and not in the election-contracting business, you re' quire to have some capital to go ahead with, and the money is put in and you do not get your drawbacks till some little time afterwards. All that should be done at that time of the year, unless a lot of money is to be thrown away, is to clear the right of way and1 take in supplies for the spring work. Everybody in the business knows that. Of course there may be a little more done. I see the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) is laughing. He knows it is true.
I know the opposite.

But it does not make any difference. Some people want to get money, and so we have another meeting of the directors of the Canadian National Railways, held in the company's offices in the city of Montreal, September 21, 1925, and I find the following:
The meeting was informed that the Rouyn Mines Railway Company has been negotiating for a loan through Dillon, Read and Company of New York of up to $2,000,000 to be secured by the pledge of not exceeding $300,000 of its thirty-year, four and a half per cent first mortgage bonds, the interest to be paid on the loan to be at the rate of four and a half per cent per annum and that one of the conditions under which said loan would be made is that payment thereof within a year would have to be guaranteed by the company, the expectation being that within such year the Rouyn Company's bonds could be sold to sufficient amount and at a reasonable rate to pay off such loan.
It was unanimously resolved that a letter in the general form submitted to the meeting or to like effect addressed to American Exchange Securities Corporation. guaranteeing payment of a loan, as above mentioned, may be executed under the corporate seal and delivered, subject to the necessary order in council.
And the report goes on. No date is given to it. I do not know when it was subsequently put through; there was no time to fill it in, anyway, when I got it in November it. is not there. A letter is written from the Canadian National Railway Company's office and it unconditionally guarantees the prompt and full repayment of all advances made under the credit, both interest and principal, in accordance with the terms of the credit. I am not going to read all the letter; it would take more time.
So there we see the guarantee of the government so satisfactorily arranged for and the pledging of the credit of the Canadian National for $2,000,000 of money. We had assurances on the floor of this House that

this sort of thing was to stop with the Scribe hotel; that there would be no more of it, and there is no more of it until the occasion arises. But it is done here, and we have the guarantee given by the Canadian National Railways of $2,000,000 to the American bankers. Over and above that we have the guarantee of the country for $3,500,000 in this rental. We have parliament deceived and flouted. Why? Why were we told during the last session that this road was to be built by capitalists? Why was it not so built? Was it again to indicate to this country that this government is careless of its word and that the country can have and ought to have no confidence in it? Surely there was a better reason. What was it? What impelling reason was there to make this government so advertise itself? And how do you think it is all done, Mr. Speaker? It is all to be carried out by this order in council, and the order in council on its face shows this government running true to form. The order in council is based on the authority of the statutes of 1915. The statute of 1915 is referred to in that order and set out in part. It is chapter 16 of the acts of that year, and under it the Minister of Railways and Canals is authorized and empowered, subject to the authority of the Governor in Council, to construct, purchase, and so on, branch lines of railway in Quebec, in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There are provisions and limitations in connection with that act. One provision is that no line which is over 200 miles in length can be acquired. The other is that the minister cannot build any line exceeding twenty-five miles in length. If we are to believe this government, having regard to their statements made day in and day out in this House, the National railways of this country are under the management and control of the Canadian Railway Board. If we are to believe what they have set out in this order in council, they are under the management and direction of the Department of Railways. It cannot be both. Either the Minister of the Interior day by day in connection with that coal question has been misleading hon. members, or this whole order in council is a farce and a sham-either one thing or the other. The only railways that can be taken under that legislation of 1915 are railways which are run in connection with or joined to what are really branches of government railways. Government railways under the definition in the act, which is the controlling act, the statute of 1915, mean any railway and all work or works connected therewith under the management and direction of the department. Will any member of the depart-

ment tell me that at any time last year the Transcontinental was under the management and direction of the department? If they do I am afraid they will prove themselves false witnesses in many cases and on many occasions. They are always saying: We have nothing to do with it; this is none of our responsibility. But for the purpose of pledging the money of the ratepayers of Canada, three and a half million dollars, oh, then they are in management, direction and control. Oh no, the Railway department could not be in control for the purpose of putting on a small twopence-halfpenny rate on fifteen thousand tons, but it can be in full control for the purpose of handling three and a half millions of dollars prior to an election.

Sir HENRY DRAYTOiN: I believe my hon. friend, not knowing where he is, is jesting with me in connection with this Rouyn railway. They could not put on a twopence-halfpenny rate, but they could pass this precious order in council. Mr. Speaker, there are sometimes when even this government cannot blow hot and cold at one and the same time. They come so close together that the wires get crossed; they are crossed now. I am pointing this out to my hon. friend. The statute of 1915 gave the (Minister of Railways, under certain terms and conditions, the right to acquire branch lines connected with the Intercolonial railway in the provinces I have mentioned, but before he had the right to get those lines, they had to be connected with the railway under the management and direction of the department. Now in answer to my hon. friend's question, I am pointing out that if we go back to the date of this statute the government could' do exactly what

he says they cannot do, namely, make rates. The government could do anything they liked about rates, and they did it on the Intercolonial, and of necessity they had to do it when the whole system was under their direction and control. Here again I am pointing out the parallel to my hon. friend, and perhaps he will be able to assist me: For the purpose of this order in council this government say that the Transcontinental is under the direction and control of the Department of Railways and Canals. They have absolutely no right, no jurisdiction to build this railway, on the one hand, or to pur-9 p.m. chase a railwa}'', on the other, unless the fact is that this Transcontinental is under the management and direction of the department, and for the purpose of this order in council they say it is under their management. The thing is really so clear that if my hon. friend did not raise the question I would apologise for labouring it, but as he has challenged me, it is just as well to labour it.
Under that act of 1915, under section 1- hon. gentlemen can read it for themselves; it is a short act-the whole right is given -by which the whole of this scheme was Con-cocted and put through, and the absolute requisite of jurisdiction is that the line from which the branch is built must be, or the line that is acquired must run to a line of railway, under the management and direction of the department. Now I wonder if all -this was forgotten by the department. I wonder if the inside practices of this government and the railway that we do not know about, although we heard a little about them the other day in connection with the men engaged on the snow work

I wonder if the inside practices of this government and the railway are so close that the government forgot altogether about the -order in council under the legislation of 1919 under which the management an-d control of this railway, the Transcontinental, was -placed in the hands of the Canadian National railway. My hon. friend the Minister -of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) nods his head. Then I -tell him his whole order in council is absolutely improper, because it is an order in -council dealing with the construction of a branch of a line which is not a government railway within the meaning of the Government Railways Act.
I also point out further, that even if that is so, even if we can have Tweedledum and Tweedledee each in turn working for the government-one moment National railways, government control, and the next instant, when it pays, Canadian National control-

The Address-Sir Henry Drayton
even if we can have that, in any event I say this is illegal, in any event it is wrong, in any event it is a scandal. I pay no further attention for the moment to what I said this afternoon as to the way in which this House was misled and tricked. This is a railway forty-five miles in length. Now there is a plain straight limitation here, so plain that he who runs may read, that nothing over twenty-five miles can be constructed except with the -approval of parliament. There is the limitation. Now is there any dispute as to the forty-five miles? Let us concede everything the whole way along. There is always something else Staring my hon. friends in the face-always. What is the answer to the plain breach of the statute except the whip of necessity, to get something done that it pays to do? Well, there we have the twenty-five miles.
We may have somebody get up in this House -and argue: Oh, the government did not build it; the government have the right to buy a railway up to 300 miles in length; they have a right to lease railways up to 200 miles in length; the government are not building. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, which hon. gentleman is going to fake that position, but he ought to be looked upon as the supreme humourist of our day if he ever thinks anyone will ever take that suggestion seriously. Here we have the government doing everything through the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National Railways having no rights at all. Here we have the trick of the lease just for the purpose of enabling the bonds to be put on. Fo-r what purpose? Because the government had no right to build the line; it had) to do it through a third party. They had no direct right to pledge the credit of the country, therefore they had to do it by way of stealth and subterfuge. Who can say that this is- not government action? Who will say that this is a real thing, a real railway company? Here we have the admission in the contract with the Noranda mines that this is indeed the work of the government, and that this government are causing this railway to be 'built. I wonder if anyone is going to- argue under those circumstances, and in view of the documents from which I have quoted, that there is any room for doubt but that this government is building this railway, and that they had to recourse to subterfuge here, there, and everywhere for the purpose o-f doing crookedly what could not be done in a straightforward manner.
Not only is the action of the government absolutely in contradiction to the statements madle to, but it is absolutely against the knowledge of, the older members of this House. It is 
another case of bad faith with parliament. This matter was discussed in 1915. The hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) knows all about it. He was in the House at the time and took -the position, following his honoured leader, that we take to-day. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals knows all about it; he was in the House at the same time and took part in the Same argument. In order -to have even a semblance of right in this matter the provisions of the Government Railways Act -have to be extended to the Transcontinental. That railway was never subject to that act; it certainly was not subject to it at the time this order w-as made. Further it was made clear in the House that under no circumstances were the enabling sections of this act of 1915 to be made use of for the purpose of justifying Such an exploitation as this of the Transcontinental railway.
Mr. Speaker, I appeal to your own recollection. You will recollect that for years we had in this country-particularly in the more easterly provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and in Quebec-branch lines which could not be run by themselves with any profit to their owners, or comfort or convenience to t'he public. The country was faced with a double set of rates, double sets of management, no through billing and the like. For years agitation was going on in the matter, and action was taken from time to time in the House. I remember reading the action taken 'by a former Minister of Railways, the late Mr. Emmerson, who I think first brought the matter up in concrete form. The whole idea was not to make possible an exploitation of the country's credit in this manner, not to open up new districts, not to have one set of rules for railway construction in one part of Canada and another set of rules for railway construction in another part of the Dominion; not to play favourites, not to pit the east against the west, Ontario against Quebec, farmers against speculators. No such use was ever intended. In those days the government had very different idea3 from what are found to-day. The matter was not left in doubt, and I refer hon. gentlemen to Hansard of 1915, when this act was up for consideration. I referred a moment ago to my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence. He took part in the discussion at that time and is reported as follows at page 1542 of Hansard of that year:
Mr. Macdonald:	While the Prime Minister is considering the amendment, I may say that I saw in one of the government papers to-day a statement to the effect that the government proposes to operate the National Transcontinental railway system as part of the Intercolonial.

I should tell the House, Mr. Speaker, that at an earlier period Sir Wilfrid Laurier had raised the question that this was a very large order and called attention to its possible effects. Mr. Macdonald goes on to say:

Island railway. That is thoroughly understood.
Why, Mr Speaker, both parties were committed to it, both parties knew what they were doing, and this government by their action are but committing another offence. The parliament of 1925 was deceived, was misled. So far as the parliament of 1915 i9 concerned, its acts are to be put to a purpose which that parliament declared they could not be put to, a declaration m which the leaders of both parties joined. Later the bill is up for third reading, and it was agreed to on what understanding? I quote from page 1685 of Hansard:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier: I understood the other day that the government policy was that this legislation was to apply only to branches of the Intercolonial.
Mr. Cochrane: Yes.
My hon. friends opposite, Mr. Speaker, indeed embarked upon a dark, twisting, tortuous adventure when they determined to set aside their own word in this House; when they determined to set at naught the statement made to members of this House and
accepted by them; when they attempt, under cover of this dummy company, manned by stenographers of the Canadian National Railways, to deceive the public; when they attempt to justify all this under an order in council, held secret until no votes could be lost through the truth being known, held secret so that all the benefits without any loss could' be had in connection with the political affiliations entered into, held1 secret until I got it in the way I have described to the House this afternoon. Ought there not to be an end some time to sham? Should we not start some time trying to deal with things on their merits? Should not even this government commence some time to have the same story for the prairies as it has for the east? Will the government, after this, again attack the Senate for holding up lines required in the prairie provinces for farmers, while at the same time they have special arrangements for their particular friends? In other words, is it really possible for a self-respecting house, irrespective of politics, irrespective of everything except decent Canadianism, to have any confidence in a government that brings down an order in council such as this, an order in council flying in the face of its obligations to this parliament and in face of the law? There are really no words which will property describe the treatment given to certain people at the hands of this government. Is this fair, right or honest?
The order in council is a long one and I propose to hand it to Hansard, as I think it is fair, not only to hon. members but to the government, that the House should see exactly what the government has done, and so that if I have misread it in any way I may be corrected. I therefore hand it to Hansard in the expectation that it will! be printed. In the same way I also hand the exhibits; it is only fair to the government and to this House that I should do so. So far as I know I have stated with absolute correctness the effect of the exhibits. I may be wrong, but if I am wrong I want to be corrected, and I can be put right only if these papers are printed properly in Hansard.
I conclude by asking the same question that I put at the commencement: Ought we to have regard for the word of a government? Ought the country to be placed in a position where it cannot tell whether the word of a government means anything or nothing? Is the word of government to-day such a light thing as to amount to nothing like the snows which have long since melted, of many winters ago? Or, has the country a right to expect that things shall be done decently and in

Mr. Speaker, had my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) confined his remarks to the question of the legality of the charter and the right to construct, 'the Rouyn railway, I would not have attempted to reply, because I have learned, through a number of years of experience in parliament, that it is useless for a layman to get into an argument with a lawyer and particularly a man well versed in railway law like my hon. friend. I have never found in the seventeen odd years that I have been in parliament that lawyers can agree amongst themselves; they can always put up a fair argument on either side of the question. But when my hon. friend attempts to show, or rather, because he did not even attempt to show, to insinuate that some grave pre-election scandal was associated with the building of this railway, I hope to convince even my hon. friend that he is very much in error in his conclusions.
Hon. members will recall that away back in 1922, 1923 and 1924, there were reports of great mineral development in the northern part of Quebec. In 1923 and 1924 particularly, reports came to us of rich finds in that part of the country, and representations were made, not only to the Canadian National Railways, but to other railways, that they should extend 
a line into that district. In 1924, Mr. Timmins of the Hollinger mines approached the president of the Canadian National Railways urging him to build a line into that section of the country. A survey was made but the railway directors and the president were not satisfied that the building of a road in there would be a profitable venture.
Shortly afterwards another discovery was made of the Noranda mines and again they were approached to build a road. Representations were such that engineers were sent there to make a very careful survey of the possibilities of that section of country. It was discovered that there were very rich mineral deposits and there was a rush not only of miners, but of railways to get into that district. It is well known that an Ontario railway that has made it very profitable to the province at large by going into the mining country was anxious to build a line, and other railway companies were similarly anxious. The Canadian National Railways made a survey, and on reports made to them it was indicated that it was questionable whether, even with the prospects of building a 500 ton smelter, the road would pay at first. The government of Quebec was approached. The people of Quebec, like the people of Toronto, appeared to be anxious that feeders going into this district should be feeders running into their different cities. I am not going into that because it is natural that each should want to get the business. The government of Quebec were asked for a railway land grant and they said: We will not give you a railway land grant, but we will give you a grant of some $.50,000 a year. I will come to that a little later on. Early in the summer of 1925 a location survey was made of this road, because of additional proof coming out of rich findings in that part of the country.
By what engineers was the survey made?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By the engineers of the Canadian National Railways.
That is right.

Now, Sir, as said a moment ago the funds for the construction of this railway are not being provided by the government of Canada, but by a banking institution in New York. The directors I have named represent that institution. Before undertaking to operate the road the chairman and board of directors of the Canadian National Railways secured an agreement from the government of the province of Quebec that it would give a bonus of $50,000 a year for five years, and from the Noranda mines that they would give an additional bonus of $20,000 a year for five years, or a total bonus of $70,000 a year for thai period. The traffic experts have carefully surveyed and investigated the local conditions, and they estimate that the road will carry itself with this subsidy, and that within five years at most it will return a profit to the company. Because it must not be forgotten that every person familiar with the mineral resources of that country agrees that the prospects of a railway being a profitable undertaking are exceedingly good. That is why there was not only a rush of miners into the district, there was also an attempted rush of railways. I do not say that my hon. friend is finding fault because the road which the nation had to take over and operate got a branch line into the Rouyn district before any Ther roads, but I appeal to the good sense of my hon. friend as a railway man to bear me out when I say that a trunk line railway cannot pay unless it has feeders. This line looks like a pretty good feeder for the Canadian National Railways.
Let me remind the House that the government does not undertake to say where railways are to be built. It accepts the advice of the chairman and directors of the Canadian National Railways on railway policy. And is there anyone in this House who will say that the chairman of the Canadian National Railways is not a good railway man? He has had his certificate of ability not only from the railway officials throughout the country: he is acknowledged by my right hon. friend

Well, what more does the House want? I say hon. members can have something more. This matter might properly be referred to the House Committee on Railway Estimates that is appointed each year. There hon. members will have an opportunity of calling in Sir Henry Thornton, the traffic experts and the auditors, and we will invite the fullest and freest examination into the accounts of this railway that is to be leased by the Canadian National Railways.

Mr. Speaker, when I left the chamber this afternoon the House was discussing the motion of the member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) that the previous question should be put as soon as possible, that is. as soon as allowed by hon. gentlemen opposite. As I may be absent from the House to-morrow, I should like to say in a few words what my position is on that motion, and what vote I will cast if it comes to a division when I am here. I do not purpose to take up any of the arguments that have been raised either before or during this debate. I shall merely confine myself to the attitude which I feel I must take in regard to the motion.
I gave my vote to maintain this government in power in preference to the opposition. That was in absolute accord with the attitude I took before the people who elected me to this House. Secondly, I voted against all amendments proposed by the opposition, which appeared to me as mere catching motions for election purposes, and I propose to do so in future. Were hon. gentlemen opposite on this side of the House, in the same position as my hon. friends to my left, I would do exactly the same thing. I also voted in favour of the motion made by the government to adjourn the House after the Address is adopted, because the ministers claim that they must have a recess to enable them to reorganize their government and to carry out the mandate which has been given to them, temporarily at least, by this House.
Now, Sir, it is one of two things: either the government needs that adjournment, or it does not. If the government requires that adjourn' ment, then it should take the means to obtain it. If it does not require it, I do not think it should shelter itself behind what I would call a side motion, which does not bring on the adjournment. I said at the time I voted for the adjournment that the House would be transformed into an electoral committee,
[Mr. Robb.3
and there would be no use in our being here.
I think this has been amply justified. But I do not think the motion of the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) at all advances the position of the government or the affairs of the country, nor does it give the House a chance to do anything useful; therefore I propose to vote against that motion. If the government needs the adjournment, I am prepared to vote for a straight motion for closure, which they should bring in if they require it. If they do not require it, then why take advantage of a process which simply lengthens the debate, and, although it prevents hon. members on the other side or hon. members of any group in this House from presenting further amendments to the Address leads us nowhere.
Some references have been made on one side or the other about liberty of speech. Quite so: liberty of speech, if it leads to something, is very desirable; but if I read well what is in the minds of the people outside of this House, I think they are more concerned about parliament doing something than about members of parliament talking individually or collectively. I do not begrudge either party all the advantage they may take; but I humbly submit that there is more at stake in the present situation than either the fate of the Liberal party or of the Conservative party.
I have been out of this House for many years. I have kept in contact with people who, I think, have a public conscience, and who are becoming disinterested more and more from day to day and more separated from party shibboleth, from party spirit. It is not, I repeat, the fate of the Liberal party or of the Conservative party whidh is at stake: it is the confidence of the people in the usefulness of our public institutions. We have been here a month and a half. I have indulged in my share of the sin of talking, but I do not propose to repeat that sin too often, or to make the sin too heavy. Therefore, I simply state to-night that I do not think the motion of the hon. member for Nelson will lead us to any practical point. I do not begrudge him the right to make his motion, and I do not dispute the sincerity of his purpose. I do not try to ascertain whether he is acting under agreement with the government or not. I take him at his word. I believe in his word of honour, and as a matter of fact I believe that if he had consulted the government they would have advised him he was not rendering them a service by proposing that motion.
No, no.

Well, at least, that is my point of view. I do not think the government

Mr. W. \\ . KENNEDY (Winnipeg South Centre): Probably I could suggest to the hon. member for Labelle (Mir. Bourassa) an answer to the question which he has propounded to this House. He advances the argument that the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) could not have sought counsel with the government in taking the action that he did, because if he had done so, and if they wanted to close the discussion in this House, they would have introduced closure and would not have adopted closure by the less direct method. I should like to say if the hon. member has followed the conduct of this government in the past four years he would have observed that the record of the government is neither one of courage, nor of direct action. This is not a government having the courage to do what it wants to do, but as enunciated by its leader, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, on many platforms. it believes in the policy of the middle way, the policy of political expediency; J suggest to the hon. member for Labelle that perhaps, following that same policy by which it has been guided for four years, the same policy which has put it into the dilemma in which it finds itself to-night, by virtue of that same sort of policy it finds itself supporting the motion of the hon. member for Nelson.
In view of what the hon. member for Labelle. an old and distinguished member of
this House, has said as to prolonging this discussion, I naturally feel, as a new member, a little diffident about continuing the discussion further. But, Sir, were it not for the circumstances under which the government of the day seeks to adjourn this House, I would not at this late day and at this late hour take part in the debate. What are the circumstances under which the government seeks to adjourn the House? A committee of this House is investigating the gravest charges which have ever been preferred, I understand, in this House of Commons for two generations and under these circumstances the government asks this House to adjourn, and, as I am informed, to leave that committee without the power to function effectively. If there were no other reason beyond that, Sir, I submit that that in itself is reason enough, not only for members on this side but for members in all quarters of this House, to take part in this debate with the object and with the intent that this government shall continue to sit; that this parliament shall continue in session so that witnesses may be examined here and be forced to give the evidence which is necessary in order that the committee may effectively proceed.
Mr. Speaker, in venturing into this debate I am conscious of many handicaps which are normally incident to the first effort of a new member of this House. Some thirty years ago I believe, Sir, you yourself, were in the position of a new member, and like myself, "with all your troubles to come." Perhaps when I recall those days to you, you will be able to recall some of the handicaps to which I refer.
Let me say, first, that there is borne in upon me at the beginning of my speech a consciousness of the comparative futility of talking at all. I say that for this reason: I have heard in this House, and you have heard, members of this parliament of mature experience bring forward matters of national interest and of national concern, bring them forward and elucidate them with outstanding ability; yet when the time came to vote no weight of argument, no amount of logic, no reason would stand up against the crack of the party whip. Does this House desire an illustration? I will give it two. We had, in the first instance, in this House a motion tantamount to a motion of want of confidence in the government. We heard expressions of opinion from all corners of this House; we speculated naturally as to the result. I for one when I heard the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) declare that she had no confidence in this government, thought: "There

is one against them". But like many others, I counted wrong. When I heard stated in this House the opinion of the government entertained by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), and as expressed by him before he came down to this House, I thought: Well, the hon. member for Rosetown will not vote confidence in this government-and so with many others. Yet when the time for division came, all but five of the Progressive group in this House-and mark you, all but five of those hon. members who throughout the campaign recently closed talked and fought against this government and declared to their constituents that they had no confidence in it

all but five of them stood up in this House and voted confidence in the government.
In passing, let me remark as to the attitude taken by these five, without naming them. Within so short a time as I have been in politics I have come to realize that it takes considerable courage to get up in this House and vote against your party; and when five members of that group virtually take issue with the other members of it, I must say that I find only admiration for their courage.
One other example. We had a vote yesterday on the question of the treaties contracted by this government. Everyone in this House is aware that the amendment voted on referred particularly to the Australian treaty. I am informed and believe it is correct that when the same Australian treaty came up for discussion before in this House every one of the present members of the Progressive party who then sat in this House voted against it; yet when 'the vote came yesterday they all voted tantamount to endorsation of the treaty.
If appears, therefore, that argument is futile; but if futility of argument as affecting the result were a conclusive reason as to whether or not a man would speak in this House, I submit that the record would not
10 p.m. contain nearly the number of speeches that it does; and when I say that I refer not to one side of the House alone.
Another handicap. Sir, is the attitude, of which I do not complain, of the members opposite, and it applies to a new member speaking either on this side of the House or on the other side. A new member realizes that he is facing old and experienced parliamentarians who are watching, perhaps in a kindly way, but nevertheless watching his every step, and as he proceeds, questions apparently innocent in themselves are propounded with the object that the feet of the unwary may be trapped. The only armour
fMr. W. W. Kennedy.*
that a man can carry against such tactics is the armour of belief in his cause and sincerity in the arguments he puts forward. I hope, Sir, whatever else I may be accused of, that hon. members in all parts of this House will concede to me when I am through at least this measure of merit, that I have tried to be fair in my discussion of this Address.
There is also the matter of one's friends. After ailL, one's friends have a right to be critical, and they are.
Through the obscurity of all this maze of difficulties there comes one beckoning light. That, Sir, is the kindly features and the gracious mien of the honourable and honoured Speaker of this House. It may be a platitude to say that first impressions are lasting, but in this case it is indeed fortunate, for whether my time in this House be long or short, I shall carry with me always pleasant memories of your attitude towards the young members of this House, and of the kindly reception accorded to new members by this House on all sides and from all quarters.
I had heard, Sir, before the election and during the campaign something of the Liberal party. I had heard some pretty harsh things about them. I had heard too about many hon. gentlemen opposite whom I now see, but I have since learned not to think so badly of them, and, Sir, having become acquainted with you, by virtue of your position, perhaps a 'little better than with most of the others, I am encouraged to hope that, as you came from out among their ranks, perhaps when we get a little better acquainted we shall find many, many other hon. gentlemen whom we shall be delighted to know. I have met some of the hon. members outside of this House, and it has been a distinct pleasure. I must remark though, Sir, that in this House they seem to be an entirely different kind of people from what they are outside. Outside, in the corridors or at meat, they are human, likeable, lovable, but here they seem to be operating under some strain, under some handicap, under some overshadowing cloud. Then I endeavoured to speculate as to what the reason might be, as under the caucus system, no one outside of one's own caucus is allowed to know what takes place at those meetings. It has occurred to me that it might be because of this irksome alliance which they seem to have made with the Progressive party.
